prompt.brief: Design upload, version, sync, sharing, and durable file storage so users can upload and share a file reliably at scale.
successSignals: Define the source of truth for object versions and permissions and make retries idempotent.
Use bounded, partitioned state to meet 100M users and 1PB of new objects per day and metadata p95 <=150ms.
Separate the critical request path from chunk assembly, virus scanning, indexing, and replication.
Explain consistency, failure recovery, authorization, observability, and a degraded mode.

functional: Support the core workflow to upload and share a file.
Expose status, results, and freshness appropriate to upload, version, sync, sharing, and durable file storage.
Support authorization, validation, updates, deletion, and recovery semantics.
nonFunctional: Meet metadata p95 <=150ms under normal load.
Scale to 100M users and 1PB of new objects per day without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: 100M users and 1PB of new objects per day
Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

architecture.title: Distributed File Storage control-plane architecture
architecture.summary: Design upload, version, sync, sharing, and durable file storage so users can upload and share a file reliably at scale. The design separates versioned desired state from leased reconciliation work and provider mutations, making drift, retries, approvals, and audit history explicit while keeping operators responsive during execution backlogs.

deepDives.title: Desired versus observed state
points: Keep distributed file storage desired state separate from provider-observed state and show both to operators.
Make every reconciliation step conditional and resumable so a worker crash does not restart unsafe effects.
Version policy and resource state so old operations cannot overwrite newer intent.

deepDives.title: Provider failures and unknown outcomes
points: Use provider-specific idempotency tokens and query-after-timeout behavior for distributed file storage operations.
Bound retries with exponential backoff, circuit breakers, and per-provider quotas.
Route irreconcilable drift to an approval or quarantine path instead of retrying forever.

deepDives.title: Blast radius and operations
points: Partition distributed file storage work by tenant, region, cluster, or resource class and cap concurrent mutations.
Audit who changed desired state, which policy allowed it, and what provider evidence was observed.
Alert on drift age, operation backlog, failed steps, policy denials, and stale observations.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull reconciliation
tradeoffs.recommendation: Use event triggers for fast response and periodic scans for missed events, drift, and recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: A push-only distributed file storage controller silently misses changes when a provider event is lost.

tradeoffs.title: Central control plane versus provider-native controllers
tradeoffs.recommendation: Keep policy, intent, and audit centralized while isolating provider-specific application logic behind adapters.
tradeoffs.caution: A monolithic controller becomes hard to scale and couples unrelated provider failure domains.

tradeoffs.title: Automatic repair versus approval
tradeoffs.recommendation: Automate low-risk, reversible distributed file storage changes and require approval for destructive or high-blast-radius operations.
tradeoffs.caution: Full automation without policy or blast-radius controls can turn a transient signal into a widespread outage.

commonMistakes: Treating a distributed file storage API response as proof that the provider has reached the desired state.
Overwriting desired state with stale observed state after an out-of-order worker response.
Retrying timed-out provider mutations without an idempotency token or status lookup.
Running every tenant or region through one queue and allowing a hot failure domain to block all work.
Omitting policy version, operator identity, provider evidence, and drift age from the audit trail.

followUps.question: How do you handle a distributed file storage provider timeout?
followUps.answer: Persist the operation as unknown, query provider state using the idempotency token, and only retry or compensate after the result is known.

followUps.question: How do you stop a bad rollout?
followUps.answer: Use policy gates, concurrency limits, canary scopes, operation cancellation, and a versioned last-known-good desired state.

followUps.question: How do you detect drift?
followUps.answer: Compare periodic provider observations with desired state, record the observed version and age, and route policy-compliant repair separately from manual exceptions.

rubric.description: The answer addresses the distributed file storage workflow, scale, latency, durability, authorization, and failure contract.
The answer identifies the authoritative distributed file storage state, versioning or deduplication boundary, and how derived views converge.
The answer partitions distributed file storage traffic, isolates hot keys, and moves fan-out, retries, or rebuilds behind bounded asynchronous work.
The answer names freshness, backlog, error, cost, and recovery signals tied to the distributed file storage user experience.
